'''''Pentanema squarrosum''''' (syn. ''Inula conyzae''), '''ploughman's-spikenard''', is a species of [[plant]] in the [[Asteraceae]] found in Europe, North Africa, and the [[Near East]]. It is an aromatic herb that grows in calcareous grassland and was in the past sometimes harvested as a substitute for true spikenard, or nard, ''[[Nardostachys|Nardostachys jatamansi]]''.

==Description==
Ploughman's spikenard is a softly hairy plant up to about 130 cm tall with a much-branched, often purplish stem and an irregularly thickened [[taproot]]. The leaves and roots are aromatic, especially in spring, with a faint spicy, cinnamon or cumin smell. It is usually a biennial or short-lived [[perennial plant|perennial]], with an overwintering rosette.<ref name=Grieve>{{cite book |last=Grieve |first=Maud |title=A Modern Herbal |year=1972|orig-year=1931 |publisher=Dover Publications Inc. |location=New York |isbn=0-486-22798-7}}</ref><ref name=Sell2006>{{cite book |last1=Sell |first1=Peter |last2=Murrell |first2=Gina |title=Flora of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 4 ''Campanulaceae'' - ''Asteraceae'' |year=2006 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge}}</ref>

The leaves are softly furry with long, simple hairs that are thicker on the veins than on the lamina. The basal leaves are up to 15 cm long, ovate to lanceolate and slightly pointed at the tip, with a short [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] that clasps the stem ("semiamplexicaul"). The upper leaves are gradually smaller and narrower, with shorter petioles, and the topmost are sessile.

Flowering occurs in late summer. The [[inflorescence]] is a loose corymbose [[panicle]] of [[Pseudanthium|capitula]] on long stalks. Each capitulum, or flowerhead, has many rows of purple phyllaries (bracts) around the outside and a dense cluster of tiny yellow flowers in the middle. The outer flowers are female and have 3 lobes with slightly elongated rays, or ligules, to about 9 mm and a forked style. The inner ones are 7 mm long with 5 lobes, bisexual with 5 fused stamens and a forked style. 
[[File:Pentanema squarrosum Wye.jpg|thumb|Inflorescence of Ploughman's spikenard]]

The fruit is an [[achene]] about 2 mm long with a pappus of white, 8 mm hairs.<ref name=Stace2019>{{Cite book |last=Stace |first=C. A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |publisher=C & M Floristics |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2 |edition=4th |location=Middlewood Green}}</ref><ref name="Sell2006" />
[[File:Inula conyzae sl13.jpg|thumb|The fruit is an achene.]]

==Identification==
When flowering, ploughman's spikenard presents few problems of identification, but the basal leaves strongly resemble those of [[Digitalis purpurea|foxglove]]. Although these two species do not grow together, it can be difficult to identify them correctly. Ploughman's spikenard has softly hairy leaves with usually entire (not toothed) margins (or sometimes with teeth that are tipped by a prominent hydathode) and, of course, a distinct fragrance, at least in spring and summer.<ref name=Rich1998>{{cite book |last1=Rich |first1=T. C. G. |last2=Jermy |first2=A. C. |title=Plant Crib 1998 |year=1998 |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |location=London |isbn=0-901-158-28-3}}</ref><ref name=Poland2009>{{cite book |last1=Poland |first1=John |last2=Clement |first2=Eric |title=The Vegetative Key to the British Flora |year=2009 |publisher=John Poland |location=Southampton |isbn=978-0-9560144-0-5}}</ref>
[[File:Pentanema squarrosum basal leaves.jpg|thumb|The basal leaves of ploughman's spikenard resemble those of foxglove.]]

==Taxonomy==
The original name (basionynm) for this species was ''Conyza squarrosa'', assigned by [[Carl Linnaeus|Linnaeus]] in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' in 1753.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Linné |first=Carl von |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/84236 |title=Species plantarum : exhibentes plantas rite cognitas ad genera relatas, cum diferentiis specificis, nominibus trivialibus, synonymis selectis, locis natalibus, secundum systema sexuale digestas |last2=Linné |first2=Carl von |date=1753 |publisher=Junk |volume=t.2 (1753) |location=Berlin}}</ref> In this he quotes an earlier polynomial in ''[[Hortus Cliffortianus]]'', ''Conyza foliis lanceolatis acutis, caule annuo corymboso'' ("the fleabane with spear-shaped, pointed leaves and an annual, corymbose stem"). Another old name for it was ''Conyza major vulgaris'' ("the big, common fleabane"), in [[Gaspard Bauhin|Bauhin's]] ''Pinax theatri botanici ''(1623). Linnaeus described it simply as growing in dry places in Germany, Belgium, Britain and France.

In 1985 it was renamed ''Inula conyzae'' by [[Robert Desmond Meikle|Desmond Meikle]], and most publications have listed it as that until recently, but in 2019 it was renamed ''Pentanema squarrosum''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gutiérrez-Larruscain |first=David |last2=Santos-Vicente |first2=M. |last3=Martínez-Ortega |first3=M. Montserrat |last4=Rico |first4=E. |date=6 March 2019 |title=Typification of 25 names in Inula (Inuleae, Asteraceae), and a new combination in Pentanema |url=https://phytotaxa.mapress.com/pt/article/view/phytotaxa.395.1.2 |journal=Phytotaxa |language=en |volume=395 |issue=1 |pages=17–26 |doi=10.11646/phytotaxa.395.1.2 |issn=1179-3163|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The common name 'ploughman's spikenard' refers to an incense or fragrance known as [[Spikenard|nard]] (νάρδος in [[Ancient Greek]]), which is mentioned several times in the Bible as an expensive luxury item.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Spikenard from the McClintock and Strong Biblical Cyclopedia. |url=https://www.biblicalcyclopedia.com/S/spikenard.html |access-date=18 November 2025 |website=McClintock and Strong Biblical Cyclopedia Online |language=en}}</ref> The word nard comes ultimately from the Sanskrit नलद (nálada), a rare Himalayan plant called ''[[Nardostachys|Nardostachys jatamansi]]''.<ref>{{Citation |title=nard |date=1 November 2025 |work=Wiktionary, the free dictionary |url=https://en.wiktionary.org/w/index.php?title=nard&oldid=88000881 |access-date=18 November 2025 |language=en}}</ref> The addition of 'spike' to the name may be a reference to the taproot, from which the essential oil is extracted. In Europe during the Middle Ages, ploughman's spikenard would have been a cheap substitute, so called because it also has a taproot with a fragrant odour which has been described as a faint cinnamon smell.<ref name="Grieve" />

Its common names across Europe testify to its usefulness: in German it is ''Duerrwurz'' ("dried root"); in French ''Herbe aux Mouches'' ("herb of flies"). English common names include cinnamon root, great fleabane and horse heal.<ref name="Grieve" />

Its [[Ploidy|chromosome number]] is 2''n'' = 32. There are no known hybrids or subspecies.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref><ref name="Stace2019" />

==Distribution and status==
Ploughman's Spikenard is native to Europe, Western Asia and North Africa. It has also been introduced to Columbia and New Zealand.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pentanema squarrosum (L.) D.Gut.Larr., Santos-Vicente, Anderb., E.Rico & M.M.Mart.Ort. |website=Plants of the World Online |publisher=Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:60478388-2 |access-date=22 November 2025 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Pentanema squarrosum (L.) D.Gut.Larr., Santos-Vicente, Anderb., E.Rico & M.M.Mart.Ort. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/10998833 |access-date=22 November 2025 |website=Global Biodiversity Information Forum}}</ref>

It has not been evaluated for the IUCN Red List<ref>{{Cite web |title=The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species |url=https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251118165127/https://www.iucnredlist.org/ |archive-date=18 November 2025 |access-date=22 November 2025 |website=IUCN Red List of Threatened Species}}</ref> while in Britain it is classified as "least concern" because it is quite common and is not threatened.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Vascular Plant Red Data List for Great Britain (Species Status No. 7) |website=JNCC Resource Hub |url=https://jncc.gov.uk/resources/cc1e96f8-b105-4dd0-bd87-4a4f60449907 |access-date=22 November 2025 }}</ref>

In many parts of Britain, ploughman's spikenard is classified as an [[axiophyte]], which means its presence is an indication of favourable conservation status, so it is likely to be counted towards site designation (for wildlife sites, nature reserves, etc) and used in monitoring their condition.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Axiophytes |url=https://bsbi.org/learn/getting-started/terms/general-terms/axiophytes |access-date=29 November 2025 |website=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Trueman |first=Ian |date=1 January 2013 |title=The use of the axiophyte species concept to describe the ecological network of the Birmingham and Black Country of the UK West Midlands |url=https://www.academia.edu/82342856/The_use_of_the_axiophyte_species_concept_to_describe_the_ecological_network_of_the_Birmingham_and_Black_Country_of_the_UK_West_Midlands |journal=Environmental & Socio-economic Studies |doi=10.1515/ENVIRON-2015-0020|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Habitat and ecology==
Ploughman's spikenard only grows on calcareous soils over chalk, limestone or sand.  It prefers very short swards and often occurs in areas of disturbance, such as roadsides and old quarries.  It is rarely abundant and often occurs as scattered plants. In the British National Vegetation Classification, it is found in [[Calcicolous grasslands in the British National Vegetation Classification system|Calcicolous grasslands]] CG1, CG2, CG3, CG4, CG5 and CG7.<ref name=Rodwell3>{{cite book |last1=Rodwell |first1=J. S. |title=British Plant Communities, vol. 3: Grasslands and montane communities|year=1992 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge |isbn=0-521-39166-0}}</ref>
<ref name=Lockton>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015|isbn=978-0-9530937-2-4}}</ref>

Ploughman's spikenard is host to various flying insect pollinators and at least 48 parasites, including [[Orobanche picridis-hieracioidis|oxtongue broomrape]], which is very rare in Britain but more common in Europe; the [[Coleophora conyzae|spikenard case-bearer moth]], which is oligophagous on this plant and related fleabanes; and ''[[Coleosporium]] inulae'', a type of rust fungus which has part of its life cycle on pine trees and part on members of the Asteraceae.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Inula conyzae – Plant Parasites of Europe |url=https://bladmineerders.nl/host-plants/plantae/spermatopsida/angiosperma/eudicots/superasterids/asterids/campanulids/asterales/asteraceae/asteroideae/inuleae/inula/inula-conyzae/ |access-date=20 November 2025 |website=bladmineerders.nl}}</ref>

==Uses==
The dried and powdered root makes a pungent type of incense, and this is probably why it was given the name ploughman's (cf. poor man's) spikenard, although the smell is not much like true spikenard. It is also said that the dried leaves can burned and used as an insecticide and parasiticide, especially against fleas.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Doğan |first1=Hüseyin |title=Pentanema squarrosum (Gölge andızotu) |url=https://kocaelibitkileri.com/pentanema-squarrosum/ |website=Kocaeli Bitkileri |language=tr |date=16 September 2019 |access-date=22 April 2026}}</ref><ref name="Grieve" />
